title: When Your Partners Start Stealing Your Customers
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0085: Email from Jonathan Bellack to Laurent Cordier re YM Plan Docs (June 16, 2011)
excerptForBlog: Executive summary: Yield managers are disintermediating our access to inventory, inhibiting our overall display strategy. We have product and service gaps against Yield Managers. We have a plan to close those gaps and facilitate inventory flow to AdX (assuming it generates best yield). Some short-term actions will mitigate key risks. Our ask: 1) approval to our plan, 2) help to mitigate the risks. Yield Managers are a growing part of the buys on Invite Media. Yield Managers are persistent on DFP Small Business. A growing percentage of AFC+AdX publishers are working with Yield Managers, too. Premium DFP publishers are working with Yield Managers and networks. 60% of paying DFP publishers are using a third party yield manager of a competitive exchange. More than 75% of DFP pubs maintain direct network relationships.

lessonTitle: When Your Partners Start Stealing Your Customers
pullQuote: When 60% of your paying customers are already using a competitor's tool inside your own platform, you don't have a partnership problem — you have a survival problem.
leadershipTraits: Thinks in structural threats, not surface symptoms
Translates diagnosis into a concrete ask
Moves toward short-term mitigation while planning long-term fix
situation: In June 2011, Google's Jonathan Bellack sent an internal memo to Laurent Cordier laying out a serious problem: independent 'yield managers' — third-party tools that help publishers optimize ad revenue — were quietly inserting themselves between Google and the publishers Google depended on. The memo is a strategy brief asking leadership for two things: approval of a plan and help managing the risks.
insight: The document's opening line is the tell: yield managers are 'disintermediating our access to inventory.' That's a classic platform-strategy threat. Google built AdX as the exchange where ad inventory flows; yield managers sit upstream and decide where that inventory actually goes. The numbers in the memo make the exposure concrete — '60% of paying DFP publishers are using a third party yield manager of a competitive exchange,' and 'more than 75% of DFP pubs maintain direct network relationships.' Google isn't losing customers yet, but it is losing routing power. The strategic instinct here is correct: identify the chokepoint before revenue drops, not after. Bellack frames this as a product and service gap problem, which points toward a build-or-buy response to recapture the layer that intermediaries now occupy.
application: Map your own distribution stack right now. List every party that sits between your product and your end customer. If any one of them controls routing decisions for more than 30–40% of your volume and works with competitors, you have a disintermediation risk. Decide before revenue dips: do you build the capability in-house, acquire it, or negotiate exclusivity? The time to act is when the trend is visible in the data, not when it shows up in your revenue line.
